props.title: Nosferatu

sections.content: Nosferatu (1922) revolutionized horror cinema with F.W. Murnau's expressionist masterpiece, an unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's "Dracula." Max Schreck's rat-like Count Orlok remains one of cinema's most unsettling monsters - his elongated fingers, pointed ears, and hollow eyes creating a vampire archetype that influenced decades of horror. The film's use of shadows, particularly the iconic scene of Orlok's silhouette climbing the stairs, established techniques that directors like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) and Vampyr (1932) would build upon. Despite Stoker's estate demanding all copies be destroyed, Nosferatu survived to become the definitive German expressionist horror film.

sections.content: Murnau's innovative cinematography techniques revolutionized horror filmmaking. His use of negative film to create an otherworldly day-for-night effect in forest scenes, accelerated footage to make Orlok's movements unnaturally jerky, and practical effects like stop-motion for the vampire's loading of coffins influenced directors for generations. The Witch (2015) and The Lighthouse (2019) directly reference Murnau's stark compositions and unsettling atmosphere, while Let the Right One In (2008) echoes Nosferatu's blend of horror and tragic romance. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence on Modern Horror

Contemporary horror continues drawing from Nosferatu's visual language. The Babadook (2014) borrows directly from Orlok's silhouette for its monster design, while It Follows (2014) mimics Murnau's use of slow, deliberate movement to create dread. The film's emphasis on atmosphere over jump scares influenced art house horror like Under the Skin (2013) and A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night (2014), the latter explicitly paying homage to Nosferatu's vampire imagery. Even found footage films like [REC] (2007) trace their shadowy aesthetics to Murnau's groundbreaking work.
